newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: OPINION - U.S. savings ratio - By J-P Beguelin.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - U.S. savings ratio - By J-P Beguelin.

text.p: By Jean-Pierre Beguelin, chief economist, Pictet & Cie

Until recently, the message broadcast by countless pundits was unequivocal. As U.S. households were less prepared to spend more money on consumer goods because they had run up too much debt, U.S. economic growth was heading for a marked slowdown.

Sooner or later, the FED would have to trim interest rates to forestall the onset of recession. It would appear that things haven't changed much since Antiquity when Aesop's singing and the wastrel Grasshopper needed the help of the thrifty and hard-working Ant to see him through the hard winter.

But the cold facts of life are a lot more complex. Contrary to what many believe, American households are not up to their eyes in debt. According to FED statistics on the flow of funds, U.S. household assets totalled some $20 trillion in 1995 whereas their liabilities including mortgages and consumer credit stood at a mere $5 trillion. This puts U.S. households' net wealth at $15 trillion, equivalent to twice the country's GDP or almost three times the size of these households' disposable income.
This wealth is rising on the buoyancy of financial markets and was up by over 20 percent between end-1994 and mid-1996.

In principle, this should encourage U.S. households to spend more. But consumer spending has barely risen over the last six months although households' disposable income has been climbing steadily under the combined impetus of pay rises and more jobs.

There could be three reasons for this. Consumers may simply be writing off their new-found wealth as a temporary phenomenon. Secondly, householders starting to expect interest rates to fall may decide to buy high-yielding instruments. Thirdly, they may be suffering a liquidity squeze with banks refusing loans as householders' assets are tied up long-term or, in the eyes of bankers, have become too risky to be accepted as collateral.

But none of these explanations are entirely convincing. If this new-found wealth were regarded as purely temporary, then many households would be rushing to lock in gains immediately, unleashing a flood of selling that would send the prices of financial assets tumbling. This thinking might just about be viable to explain the correction on Wall Street early in July, but sits uneasily with the autumn rally in U.S. stocks.

The cash crunch theory is not very persuasive either even though it fits in neatly with the marked rise in the ratio of consumer debt to households' liquid assets, up to 31 percent by mid-1996 from 25 percent at end-1993. If banks, all of a sudden, had been refusing to lend to households then we should have seen bank interest rates climbing and the yield curve flattening out because of rising short-term interest rates, and not because of dropping long-bond yields which was the case in recent weeks.

A higher ratio of consumer credit can be due to households resorting ever more frequently to credit cards for payments. Greater use of "plastic money" has bloated the total of credit card payments yet to be settled -- a very short-term float. It is hard to see how this could alter the behaviour of households.

The third theory -- a shift in householders' perception of financial trends -- raises more questions than it answers. It is not easy to see why people would suddenly expect interest rates to fall when their disposable income is rising, their confidence in the future is high and jobs are relatively easy to find.

In a nutshell, the increase in the U.S. savings ratio in the third quarter appears to be random, a short-term blip that often plagues quarterly series like consumer spending data. The rise is likely to be soon forgotten. Taken in isolation, it does not call for any urgent intervention by monetary authorities.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters)
